seo_title: What Happens After Invoking the Appraisal Clause in Texas?
meta_description: What happens after invoking the appraisal clause in Texas: appraiser selection, umpire, inspections, the award and payment.
h1: What Happens After Invoking the Appraisal Clause in Texas? A Step-by-Step Guide
primary_keyword: invoking the appraisal clause in Texas
excerpt: Invoking appraisal starts a defined process: each side names an appraiser, an umpire is chosen, the loss is inspected and priced, and a signed award sets the amount. Here is each step in Texas.
key_takeaways: Invoking appraisal starts a structured process to settle the amount of loss, not coverage.
Each side names its own appraiser, and the two appraisers select an umpire.
Appraisers inspect, compare estimates, and resolve differences line by line.
An award signed by any two of the three is generally binding on the amount.
Payment of an award is typically due within the policy and Chapter 542 timeframes.
body_html:
After invoking the appraisal clause in Texas, each side names an independent appraiser, the two appraisers select an umpire, and the appraisers inspect the property and compare estimates. If they agree, they sign an award. If not, the umpire decides the disputed items, and an award signed by any two of the three sets the amount of loss.

What does the appraisal clause do?

The appraisal clause is a provision in most Texas homeowners and commercial property policies. It gives the policyholder and the insurer a way to resolve disagreements over the amount of loss without going to court.

Appraisal is not a lawsuit, and it is not a full arbitration of the claim. It answers one question: how much does it cost to repair or replace the covered damage? In State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009), the Texas Supreme Court held that appraisers decide the amount of loss and may consider the extent of damage and causation, but they do not decide coverage or liability.

If you are new to the concept, start with our overview of what an insurance appraisal is. This article focuses on what happens once appraisal has actually been demanded.

The appraisal process step by step

Policy wording varies, so always read your own appraisal clause. Most Texas policies follow this general sequence:

StepWhat happensTypical timing
1. Written demandOne party demands appraisal in writing.Any time a dispute over amount exists, subject to policy terms
2. Appraisers namedEach party selects a competent, disinterested appraiser.Often within 20 days of the demand
3. Umpire selectedThe two appraisers agree on an umpire.Often within 15 days; a court can appoint one if they cannot agree
4. InspectionAppraisers inspect the property and gather documents.Usually a few weeks after selection
5. Estimates comparedEach appraiser prepares or reviews estimates; differences are negotiated.Weeks to a few months
6. Umpire reviewUnresolved items go to the umpire.Only if the appraisers disagree
7. AwardA written award signed by any two sets the amount.At the conclusion
8. PaymentThe insurer pays the award, less deductible and prior payments.Per policy and Chapter 542 deadlines

Step 1–2: The demand and choosing your appraiser

Appraisal begins with a written demand that identifies the claim, states that the parties disagree on the amount of loss, and invokes the policy's appraisal provision. Either party can usually make the demand. Send it in a way you can prove delivery.

Next, each side selects its own appraiser. Most policies require the appraiser to be "competent" and "disinterested." In practice, that means someone who understands construction costs and estimating, and who does not have a financial stake in the outcome, such as a contractor who would perform the repairs.

Your appraiser advocates for an accurate amount of loss on your behalf. A good appraiser should be able to:

  • Inspect and document roof, exterior, and interior damage thoroughly
  • Build or review line-item estimates in Xactimate or Symbility
  • Explain pricing, quantities, and code items clearly to the other side
  • Present a persuasive case to an umpire if needed

Choose carefully. Your appraiser will set the tone of the negotiation, and an appraiser who cannot defend line items or explain pricing leaves money on the table. Ask about estimating experience, Texas claim history, and how they handle umpire presentations.

Step 3: How the umpire is selected

Once both appraisers are named, they try to agree on an umpire. The umpire is a neutral third party who only steps in on items the two appraisers cannot settle.

If the appraisers cannot agree within the time the policy allows, either party can usually ask a court to appoint one. In Texas, that request is typically filed in the county where the property is located. Our guide on how insurance umpires are chosen in Texas covers what makes a good umpire and how disputes over selection are handled.

Steps 4–5: Inspection, documentation, and estimates

This is where most of the work happens. The appraisers inspect the property, often together, to see the damage firsthand. They review photos, prior estimates, contractor bids, engineering reports, measurement reports, and invoices.

Each appraiser then prepares or refines an estimate of the amount of loss. Strong evidence matters here. Dated photos, moisture readings, tear-off documentation, code letters, and 3D scans all help prove what was damaged and what the repair requires. See what evidence helps during insurance appraisal for a detailed list.

The appraisers compare their estimates line by line. Many items, such as interior paint or gutter replacement, often get resolved quickly. The real negotiation tends to focus on a handful of issues: full roof replacement versus repair, matching, measurements, pricing, and code upgrades.

What you should do while appraisal is underway

  • Give your appraiser every document you have: the policy, all carrier estimates and letters, contractor bids, photos, and invoices.
  • Provide access to the property for inspections, including attics, interiors, and outbuildings.
  • Write down when damage first appeared, especially interior leaks, so the timeline is clear.
  • Avoid signing releases or accepting final payments without discussing them with your appraiser.
  • Keep paying your mortgage and policy premiums, and keep the policy in force.
Tip: Keep making normal repairs needed to prevent further damage, but photograph everything first and keep receipts. Do not tear out disputed materials until your appraiser has documented them.

Steps 6–7: Umpire review and the appraisal award

If the appraisers reach full agreement, they sign a written award and the umpire is not needed. If they agree on some items but not others, they submit the disputed items to the umpire.

The umpire reviews both sides' estimates and evidence and may inspect the property personally. The umpire then decides each disputed item, usually within the range the two appraisers presented. An award signed by any two of the three, whether both appraisers or one appraiser plus the umpire, sets the amount of loss.

Awards often itemize replacement cost value, depreciation, and actual cash value, sometimes broken out by coverage, such as dwelling, other structures, and contents. That breakdown matters for depreciation recovery later. Read what happens if appraisers disagree for more on the umpire stage.

Step 8: Payment and what happens after the award

Once the award is signed, the insurer generally pays the amount owed under the policy, minus the deductible and any amounts already paid. Under Texas Insurance Code Chapter 542, once an insurer accepts a claim it generally must pay within five business days, and many carriers treat a signed award similarly. Check the deadlines with our Texas claim deadline calculator.

On replacement cost policies, the award may separate actual cash value from recoverable depreciation. You typically receive ACV first and recover depreciation after completing repairs and submitting proof.

Texas courts have addressed what happens after payment. In Barbara Technologies v. State Farm Lloyds (Tex. 2019), the court held that paying an appraisal award does not automatically bar a prompt-payment claim under Chapter 542. In Ortiz v. State Farm Lloyds (Tex. 2019), it held that payment of an award generally bars most other extra-contractual claims. This is general information, not legal advice; consult a Texas attorney about legal rights.

Texas-specific considerations during appraisal

Texas policyholders should keep a few state-specific points in mind:

  • Weather claims are common. Most appraisals in Texas involve hail and wind, from the Panhandle to Central Texas and DFW, plus hurricane claims on the Gulf Coast.
  • Chapter 542A notice. For many weather claims, a 61-day pre-suit notice is required before filing a lawsuit, which is separate from appraisal.
  • Causation can be addressed. Because appraisers may assess what damage the storm caused, appraisal is often useful when the carrier argues some damage is wear and tear.
  • Coverage stays outside appraisal. If the carrier denies coverage entirely, appraisal may not resolve that issue. See can you invoke appraisal after a denied claim.

How long does the process take?

Timing is one of the most common questions homeowners ask after invoking the appraisal clause in Texas. Our insurance appraisal timeline guide breaks the stages down further. Simple residential roof claims may be resolved in a few weeks to a few months after appraisers are named. Larger or commercial losses, claims that need an umpire, or claims with many disputed items can take longer.

The biggest factors are how quickly appraisers and an umpire are selected, access to the property, how complete the documentation is, and how far apart the estimates are. A well-documented claim almost always moves faster, because the appraisers spend less time gathering information and more time resolving actual differences.

Next steps after you invoke appraisal

Appraisal works best when you go in prepared. Gather your policy, every estimate and letter from the carrier, your contractor bids, and your photos before your appraiser's first inspection. The earlier your appraiser sees the full file, the sooner the real points of disagreement come into focus.

If you have invoked appraisal, or the insurer has, your most important decision is who will serve as your appraiser. You want someone who knows Texas construction costs, writes defensible estimates, and has spent time on the policyholder side of claims.

On an appraisal assignment, he serves as the policyholder's appraiser, building the line-item estimate and presenting it to the other side and the umpire.

faqs.q: Can my insurance company refuse appraisal in Texas?
faqs.a: If your policy contains an appraisal clause and there is a genuine disagreement over the amount of loss, the insurer generally cannot simply refuse. Disputes can arise over whether the demand was timely, whether appraisal was waived, or whether the disagreement involves coverage instead of amount. Courts in Texas typically enforce valid appraisal clauses.

faqs.q: Who pays for the appraisers and umpire?
faqs.a: Under most Texas policies, each party pays its own appraiser, and the parties split the umpire's fees and other shared appraisal costs equally. Check your policy's appraisal clause for the exact wording. Our appraisal cost calculator can help estimate whether appraisal makes financial sense for your claim.

faqs.q: Can I still talk to my insurance adjuster during appraisal?
faqs.a: You can, but most communication about the amount of loss usually flows through the appraisers once appraisal is underway. Continue responding to legitimate information requests and keep copies of everything. If the adjuster offers a revised settlement during appraisal, discuss it with your appraiser before deciding whether to accept.

faqs.q: Is an appraisal award final in Texas?
faqs.a: Generally, yes. Texas courts give appraisal awards strong deference, and an award signed by two of the three panel members usually binds both parties on the amount of loss. Courts may set aside an award in limited situations, such as fraud, accident, mistake, or an award that does not comply with the policy.

faqs.q: Can appraisal be invoked after the insurer already paid part of the claim?
faqs.a: Yes, in many cases. A partial payment often signals that the insurer accepts some covered damage but disagrees on the amount, which is exactly what appraisal addresses. The award amount is typically reduced by prior payments and the deductible. Review your policy for any time limits on demanding appraisal.
